evidence.title: Flash loan facilitated attacks
evidence.evidence_text:
A flash loan is uncollateralized, same-transaction borrowing. OWASP says flash loans are not inherently vulnerable, but they give an attacker arbitrarily large, transient capital within one transaction. Any protocol whose trust assumptions rest on capital at risk or historical position size is exposed when an attacker can hold large balances temporarily without risking their own funds. The attacker batches a transaction that borrows via a flash loan, manipulates protocol state, prices or accounting with the borrowed funds, extracts profit, and repays the loan in the same transaction. OWASP names governance voting, oracle pricing, share and accounting logic, and liquidation and collateral checks as areas to review.
Root cause: Protocol assumptions fail when an attacker temporarily controls substantial liquidity. OWASP notes that flash loans act as a force multiplier for underlying business logic, oracle, arithmetic or access control weaknesses, which must be fixed at the root. Design economic and accounting logic on the assumption that arbitrarily large, transient capital is available. Rate limit sensitive operations per block or epoch, cap exposure per interaction with limits on slippage, position sizes and borrowing, and include flash-loan scenarios in tests and fuzzing.

evidence.title: Unprotected Ether withdrawal
evidence.evidence_text:
Due to missing or insufficient access controls, malicious parties can withdraw some or all Ether from the contract account. The SWC entry notes that this bug is sometimes caused by unintentionally exposing initialization functions: if a function intended to be a constructor is named wrongly, its code ends up in the runtime bytecode and can be called by anyone to re-initialize the contract. Before Solidity 0.4.22 a constructor was a function named exactly like its contract, so a name mismatch left it a normal callable function.
Root cause: Withdrawal functions lack effective caller authorization, so the contract does not check who may trigger a transfer of Ether out. Implement controls so withdrawals can only be triggered by authorized parties or according to the specs of the smart contract system. Also check that initialization code cannot be called again by an arbitrary account. Since Solidity 0.4.22 the constructor keyword makes constructor definitions clearer than the old same-name rule. The SWC registry is no longer actively maintained, so treat its text as historical guidance.

evidence.title: Incorrect constructor name
evidence.evidence_text:
Constructors are special functions called only once, during contract creation. They perform critical, privileged actions such as setting the owner of the contract. Before Solidity 0.4.22, the only way to define a constructor was a function with the same name as the contract. A function meant to be a constructor becomes a normal callable function if its name does not exactly match the contract name, which can happen when contract code is re-used under a different name and the constructor function name is not changed. Since Solidity 0.4.22 the constructor keyword is available, and the Solidity documentation describes the constructor as a function declared with it that runs once at creation.
Root cause: A function intended as a constructor does not match the legacy contract name, so it stays callable after deployment. Upgrade the contract to a recent Solidity compiler version and change to the constructor keyword declaration, which makes constructor definitions clearer.

evidence.title: Denial of service with block gas limit
evidence.evidence_text:
Deploying a contract or calling its functions always requires gas, based on how much computation is needed. Ethereum specifies a block gas limit, and the sum of all transactions included in a block cannot exceed it. Programming patterns that are harmless in centralized applications can become a denial of service in smart contracts when the cost of executing a function exceeds the block gas limit. Modifying an array of unknown size that increases in size over time can lead to this condition.
Root cause: Required operations iterate over unbounded state, as in the growing-array case. Be cautious when large arrays are expected to grow over time, and avoid actions that require looping across the entire data structure. If a loop over an array of unknown size is absolutely necessary, plan for it to take multiple blocks and therefore multiple transactions.

evidence.title: Denial of service with failed call
evidence.evidence_text:
External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately, which can cause a denial of service in the contract. When a contract needs every call in a batch to succeed, for example payments pushed to many recipients in a loop, one failing recipient can block the whole operation. The Solidity documentation adds that sending Ether can fail because the recipient runs out of gas, including through require, assert or revert, and that with transfer or send plus a return value check this can give the recipient a way to block progress in the sending contract.
Root cause: Progress depends on every external transfer or call succeeding. Isolate each external call into its own transaction that can be initiated by the recipient of the call. This matters especially for payments: let users withdraw funds rather than pushing funds to them automatically, which also reduces the chance of problems with the gas limit. Avoid combining multiple calls in a single transaction, especially inside a loop, always assume external calls can fail, and implement the contract logic to handle failed calls.

evidence.title: Explained: The Ledger Supply Chain Incident (October 2026)
evidence.evidence_text:
In October 2026, some Ledger users were the target of a supply chain attack, where on-chain analysis estimates $93 million was stolen from accounts protected by a Ledger hardware wallet. Hardware distributed by one of the company’s resellers included components that stole recovery phrases for accounts stored on the device.
Inside the Attack
The Ledger supply chain incident was discovered on October 9, when users of the hardware wallet started reporting that funds were disappearing from their on-chain accounts. Ledger confirmed an unauthorized implant in at least one device sold by CryptoBilis, a Ledger reseller located in Southeast Asia, and its security team has since described how the implant worked.
This implant monitored the hardware wallet’s screen during setup and captured the 24-word recovery phrase that can be used to regenerate the root key for the account so the user could transfer it to another device if desired. The implant included an eSIM that allowed it to transmit the stolen recovery phrase to the attacker via LTE.
The malicious implant didn’t interact with the device’s Secure Element or any of the transaction or signing logic. However, stealing the root key undermined the security of the associated accounts since the attacker could derive any private key generated and stored on the device and steal the associated crypto.
After the attack was identified, Tether froze about $10 million in USDT. Ledger also issued guidance to users not to initialize unused CryptoBilis devices and to migrate any crypto on a CryptoBilis hardware wallet to a new device with a fresh recovery phrase. Ledger asked resellers in seven Asian markets to suspend sales and remove devices from shelves.
Devices sold by CryptoBilis are the only ones Ledger has tied to confirmed losses so far, but other reports suggest the tampering may reach beyond that reseller. On October 13, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès publicly confirmed that a Ledger Flex purchased at Singapore’s Changi Airport from retailer Metapod had been implanted with a spy module, though Ledger has not publicly confirmed a connection to the CryptoBilis cases.
A researcher also reported similar modifications in wallets bought at MediaMarkt stores in Europe, and store records he shared list a European distributor as the inventory source, but those records do not show the distributor supplied the specific wallets or took part in modifying them, and no link has been proven.
Lessons Learned from the Attack
The Ledger supply chain incident demonstrates how physical implants can bypass protections on hardware wallets. While the core Ledger circuitry and logic were unaffected, the attacker took advantage of the fact that the screen needed to display sensitive information (the recovery phrase) to the user. An implant that could also monitor the screen could steal and exfiltrate the recovery phrase, resulting in an estimated $93 million in losses.
This incident demonstrates the risks associated with extended supply chains for hardware wallets and similar devices. The compromised devices came from an authorized reseller. Buying directly from the manufacturer helps to reduce risk by limiting the number of parties with physical access to a security-critical device.

evidence.title: Ledger $93M Exploit Explained: Supply Chain Security Update
evidence.evidence_text:
Ledger $93M Exploit Explained: What You Need to Know
Imagine buying a high-tech physical safe for your home to keep your cash completely secure. But without your knowledge, someone tampered with the lock mechanism inside the factory before the safe ever reached your front door. That is essentially what crypto investors are facing right now following a major security event involving Ledger hardware wallets.
In early October 2026, news broke that crypto assets worth nearly $93 million had suddenly vanished from hundreds of user wallets. The affected funds spanned across major blockchain networks including Bitcoin (BTCBTC+0.12%), EthereumETH-1.07%, TRON (TRX), BNBBNB-0.20% Chain (BNB), and Polygon (POL).
If you store your digital assets in cold storage, this news might sound concerning at first glance. However, understanding the exact nature of this exploit is crucial. It does not appear to be a failure in Ledger's core technology or master servers. Instead, available evidence points toward a compromised physical supply chain involving an official reseller in Southeast Asia.
Let us break down everything that happened, how the stolen funds were moved across chains, what top industry figures are saying, and the exact steps you should take right now to secure your crypto.
What Happened? Understanding the $93 Million Exploit
On Friday, October 9, 2026, blockchain security researchers began detecting unusual wallet drains occurring across multiple networks simultaneously. Hundreds of individual crypto addresses were being emptied in rapid succession.
Initial estimates pegged total losses at around $72 million. However, as deep-dive forensic analysis progressed, analytics firm Bitquery revised the total losses upward to $92.9 million across 311 distinct user wallets.
The stolen funds were spread across five major blockchain networks:
- Bitcoin (BTC)
- Ethereum (ETH)
- TRON (TRX)
- BNB Chain (BNB)
- Polygon (POL)
A separate report by on-chain investigator Specter also highlighted suspicious wallet addresses receiving funds from victims across Ethereum, TRON, and Bitcoin, estimating overall damage above $86 million.
What makes this event stand out is that hardware devices like Ledger are designed specifically to keep secret recovery keys completely offline. When set up properly on a secure device, hackers on the internet cannot access those keys. But if a physical device is modified or tampered with before reaching the customer, those offline protection guarantees can be effectively bypassed.
The Suspect: A Localized Supply-Chain Attack
So how did modified devices get into the hands of crypto users? The investigation points directly to an official third-party reseller in Southeast Asia named Crypto Bilis.
Crypto Bilis is listed as an official distributor authorized to sell Ledger products in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Following reports of user losses in the region, Ledger launched an immediate investigation into products distributed by this vendor.
As a primary safety measure, Ledger requested that Crypto Bilis pause all sales and shipments of Ledger devices right away while forensic work continues.
Ledger also issued actionable guidance for anyone who recently purchased a hardware wallet through Crypto Bilis:
- Unbox / Uninitialized Devices: If you bought a device from Crypto Bilis in the last 90 days and have not set it up yet, do not set it up.
- Already Initialized Devices: If you set up a Ledger purchased from Crypto Bilis within the last 90 days, consider moving your assets to a brand-new signer with a newly generated seed phrase immediately.
"Ledger is investigating reports of loss of funds from users in South East Asia who purchased products from a reseller named Crypto Bilis. As a precaution, and pending the results of our investigation, we have asked Crypto Bilis to pause all sales and shipments of Ledger devices," the company stated in an official update.
Ledger clarified that its internal systems and central security infrastructure remain completely intact. The incident appears restricted to physical tampering within the local distribution pipeline.
How the Exploit Was Executed: On-Chain Clues
Stealing nearly $93 million across multiple blockchains requires extensive planning. On-chain analysis by Bitquery revealed fascinating structural patterns behind the transfers.
First, the exploit was not a sudden impulse attack. Researchers identified small test transactions occurring roughly two weeks prior to the major asset drain. This indicates the perpetrators were verifying access before executing their main operation.
Second, when the heavy drains began, the transactions were executed in highly synchronized batches. Multiple target wallets signed identical transaction requests within seconds of each other across distinct blockchain networks.
This automated precision suggests that the attacker possessed direct access to private keys or recovery phrases. With that access, automated scripts were programmed to broadcast withdrawal transactions simultaneously.
While public blockchains clearly document where and when funds move, on-chain data alone cannot prove how the secret seed phrases were leaked. Physical hardware analysis is required to confirm how the compromise happened on a device level.
Industry Leaders React: Insights from CZ and Mark Karpelès
Key figures across the crypto industry responded quickly to the news, offering technical perspective and advice for affected users.
Changpeng Zhao (popularly known as CZ), founder of Binance, commented on social media regarding the incident. He emphasized that available evidence pointed to a localized supply-chain problem rather than a systemic core software flaw at Ledger.
"Beware if you use a Ledger hardware wallet, especially if you bought one recently. Based on information so far, it seems to be localized to a supply chain attack with one vendor. A small number of people probably bought fake (or tampered) Ledgers," CZ noted.
CZ reaffirmed that Ledger remains one of the most established hardware wallet companies in the industry. He called on players across the BNB ecosystem and the broader crypto community to help track down and recover the stolen assets.
Meanwhile, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès shared concrete physical evidence after inspecting a suspicious Ledger Nano X device that originated from Malaysia.
According to Karpelès, the outer plastic shrink-wrap on the box looked completely factory-fresh and untampered. However, upon opening up the hardware casing, he discovered a rogue electronic module hidden inside the space usually reserved for screen padding.
This finding illustrates how advanced physical supply-chain implants have become. By inserting tiny malicious components directly into hardware circuits, bad actors can secretly log user inputs or transmit seed phrases back to remote servers.
Ledger has not yet formally confirmed whether the specific module discovered by Karpelès was directly tied to the $92.9 million theft. However, it provides a very plausible technical scenario for how hardware tampering operates in practice.
Where Is the Money Now? The Multi-Chain Fund Trace
Once stolen assets hit the blockchain, security teams and law enforcement agencies work quickly to track and freeze what they can. Here is where the stolen funds stood shortly after the exploit:
1. $10 Million USDT Frozen by TetherUSDT+0.06%
Tether acted quickly by freezing approximately $10 million in USDT across 20 wallet addresses linked to the suspect. While freezing stops those funds from being transferred or converted by the attacker, legal mechanisms are still required to return those assets to rightful owners.
2. Unmoved Assets Sitting in Attacker Wallets
Bitquery's analysis showed that a large portion of stolen funds remained parked in suspected attacker wallets:
- Around 14,810 ETH remained sitting in designated Ethereum wallets.
- Approximately 203.8 BTC remained stationary in associated Bitcoin addresses.
3. Mixing Services and USDCUSDC+0.00% Movements
The attackers also attempted to cover their tracks using privacy tools. Analysts traced roughly 1,254 ETH passing through Tornado Cash and Zcash.
Some of those laundered funds later appeared in three fresh wallets, including one address holding about 2.1 million USDC. Depending on findings by stablecoin issuer Circle and law enforcement requests, those USDC balances could potentially be frozen as well, though freezes require formal verification.
Essential Steps to Keep Your Hardware Wallet Safe
This incident highlights a fundamental lesson: keeping your crypto secure requires safe practices not just online, but throughout the entire physical purchasing journey.
Here are crucial steps to ensure your cold storage remains protected:
- Buy Direct from Official Manufacturers: Whenever possible, order hardware wallets directly from the official manufacturer's website rather than third-party merchants or online marketplaces.
- Never Use Pre-Generated Seed Phrases: A genuine hardware wallet will always generate a fresh set of recovery words on its built-in display during first setup. If a device comes with a pre-printed card containing words, it is a scam.
- Inspect Physical Condition: Check your device for unusual seams, loose plastic, or signs of tampering upon unboxing.
- Migrate Assets If Concerned: If you bought a hardware wallet from an unverified distributor or feel doubtful about its safety, transfer your funds to a safe temporary wallet right away.
- Keep Firmware Up to Date: Use official management software (such as Ledger Live) to update your device firmware regularly.
Final Summary and Industry Takeaway
The $92.9 million exploit serves as a stark reminder that physical supply chain integrity is just as vital as cryptographic security. While hardware encryption effectively shields private keys from remote network attacks, physical devices remain vulnerable if modified prior to reaching the end user.
Ledger's ongoing investigation, alongside quick intervention from asset issuers like Tether, marks the first step in addressing this breach. As forensic teams continue examining tampered devices and tracing funds across chains, further updates will follow.
For everyday crypto users, remaining proactive, buying directly from trusted sources, and inspecting hardware devices remain the best practices for safeguarding digital wealth.
Disclaimer: Past performance of digital assets or market operators is not indicative of future results. Digital asset investments carry market risks and price volatility. Always perform your own thorough research before making financial decisions.

evidence.title: Ledger users reportedly drained of over $86 million in suspected exploit
evidence.evidence_text:
Ledger logo by Wikimedia contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0
Ledger users reportedly drained of over $86 million in suspected exploit
On-chain analyst Specter traced stolen funds across Ethereum, TRON and Bitcoin, while Ledger has yet to comment publicly.
Hardware wallets exist for one reason: to keep your crypto safe when everything else goes wrong. On October 9, 2026, that promise reportedly took a serious hit.
On-chain analyst Specter (@SpecterAnalyst) flagged what appears to be a coordinated drain of funds from Ledger hardware wallet users. Cumulative losses are estimated at over $86 million, and some reports suggest the final figure could approach $100 million.
The cause has not been confirmed. Ledger has not said anything publicly.
What the on-chain trail shows
According to Specter’s analysis, the theft spans three major networks: Ethereum, TRON and Bitcoin. The analyst traced several theft addresses that received inflows from hundreds of victim wallets, pointing toward a coordinated campaign rather than a handful of unlucky individuals.
One Bitcoin address linked to the theft stands out: bc1qjqgwejnp8dc0x2938x9n9954hj97t82unx49dl. It has reportedly received over 211 BTC, and as of the report, those coins had not moved.
The big unanswered question: how
Right now, nobody outside the attacker knows exactly how the funds were taken. Discussion on X and Reddit has filled the vacuum with several theories.
The leading possibilities floated by the community include:
The news moving money, markets, and the world—before your day starts.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
Device flaws: a vulnerability in Ledger’s hardware or firmware itself.
Seed phrase compromises: the seed phrase is the list of words that can recreate a wallet anywhere. If attackers obtained those words, the device itself becomes irrelevant.
Phishing: tricking users into signing malicious transactions or handing over their recovery words through fake apps or websites.
Ledger has not confirmed any vulnerability related to its devices or firmware and had stayed silent publicly as of the report date.
A rough year for hardware wallet security
Earlier this year, a fake Ledger Live app appeared on the Apple App Store. It drained approximately $9.5 million from more than 50 users before the scheme came to light.
Separately, a flaw in the Zilliqa Ledger app led to considerable losses for users holding ZIL.
In August 2026, a reported seed-generation flaw in Coldcard hardware wallets resulted in losses exceeding $88 million in Bitcoin. The reported Ledger losses of over $86 million sit in the same range as the Coldcard incident from just two months earlier.
What this means for users
Until the attack vector is confirmed, every user has to assume some level of risk. If the root cause turns out to be phishing or a compromised third-party app, the fix is behavioral: verify software sources, never type a seed phrase into a computer or phone, and scrutinize every transaction before signing. If it turns out to be a device or firmware problem, the response becomes far more complicated, potentially involving firmware updates or migrating funds to new wallets entirely.
Several things are worth watching from here. First, whether Ledger issues an official statement identifying the cause. Second, whether the attacker begins moving the 211 BTC sitting in the flagged Bitcoin address. Third, whether the loss estimate settles closer to $86 million or climbs toward the $100 million mark as more victims are identified.

evidence.title: Ledger Exploit Explained: What Ex Mt.Gox CEO Found - Crypto News
evidence.evidence_text:
Ledger Exploit Explained: What Ex Mt.Gox CEO Found, and How to Protect Your Crypto
Ledger confirmed the exploit; at least one device linked to the CryptoBilis wallet-drain investigation contained an unauthorized hardware implant, with the estimated potential losses reaching $93 million across 311 wallets on five chains. The finding also confirms physical tampering in one affected device, for now.
In an update, Ledger said it had examined a device belonging to an impacted user and found an unauthorized hardware implant. The affected customers had purchased devices through CryptoBilis, a reseller serving Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
Ledger said it had contacted affected users and begun working with authorities on this exploit. It also asked CryptoBilis to stop selling all hardware-wallet inventory while the investigation continues, rather than suspending sales of Ledger products alone.
The company’s statement that its systems and services show no sign of compromise points toward a potential physical or reseller-side exposure, not a confirmed breach of Ledger’s backend. That narrows one part of the investigation.

One Ledger Exploit and Ex Mt. Gox CEO Finding
Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès began investigating the Ledger incident on October 9, 2026, after receiving a Ledger Nano X from Malaysia that he suspected had been physically tampered with. Despite its apparently intact shrink-wrap packaging, Karpelès said he discovered a hidden electronic module concealed behind the screen, where the device’s cushioning normally sits.
Karpelès reported that the suspected implant contained a microcontroller, LTE cellular hardware, an antenna, and an eSIM, with connections to the device’s display circuitry. He believes this configuration could allow the module to capture recovery phrases displayed during wallet setup and transmit the information over a cellular connection.
He also subsequently began examining the component more closely and called on CryptoBilis to inspect unsold inventory for similar modifications. Ledger later confirmed finding an unauthorized hardware implant inside an affected customer’s device
The wider security concern points to the reseller channel: customers may trust a device based on its brand and point of sale, while the confirmed finding shows that at least one device connected to this investigation had been physically altered.

CryptoBilis Sold to Unknown Buyer?
CryptoBilis’ ownership change has added another layer to the ongoing Ledger hardware wallet investigation. According to reports, the company’s former co-founders, Arravind Prabu and Vimalatheethan, said they completed the sale in March 2026 and handed over operational control.
However, they claimed a confidentiality agreement prevented them from publicly announcing the transaction until mid-October. The timing has attracted attention because the reports of crypto exploits involving Ledger devices sold through CryptoBilis emerged in October.
Corporate records cited by BitPinas reportedly show that 100% of CryptoBilis’ shares were transferred to an individual identified as Jiaming on August 3, 2026. The registered address associated with the buyer was reportedly in Heilongjiang province, China.
The ownership transfer is particularly relevant following former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès’ discovery of a suspected hardware implant inside a Ledger Nano X. Funny enough, 假名 (jiǎmíng) means false name in Chinese when written in those characters.
For now, investigators still need to establish how the modified devices entered circulation, who installed the components, and whether the ownership change had any connection to the attack. However, there is currently no established evidence linking CryptoBilis’ new owner to the alleged tampering.
European MediaMarkt Report and What Should You Do?
A separate community report alleged that a Ledger bought through MediaMarkt in Europe showed signs of a possible hardware exploit. MediaMarkt is an official Ledger reseller in several European markets, including Germany and Austria, but Ledger has not confirmed that the reported device was compromised or connected it to the CryptoBilis investigation.
Observers also disagreed over what the circulated images showed: some questioned whether the hardware appeared consistent with a genuine Ledger board, while others said they could not identify the same type of implant found in Southeast Asia.
Anyone who owns a Ledger hardware wallet should take this incident as a reminder to review their wallet security, even if they purchased their device directly from Ledger or another authorized retailer. There is currently no conclusive evidence that every Ledger device is affected, so owners should avoid panic and follow official security updates.
Never enter your recovery phrase on a website, in an app, or in a customer support chat, and never share it with anyone claiming to be from Ledger. If your device shows signs of physical tampering, stop using it and contact Ledger support through its official website. A genuine device check alone should not be treated as proof that the hardware has never been modified.
Owners can follow Ledger’s official genuine-check instructions to verify their device’s authenticity. However, passing this check does not guarantee that the device has never been physically tampered with, so users should also watch for signs of modification and follow official security updates. Check Ledger hardware integrity check here.
Hardware wallets purchased through questionable supply chains deserve particular scrutiny, but even owners of unaffected devices should maintain secure offline backups, verify transaction details on the device’s display, and consider a small test transfer before moving substantial funds.
Above all, never wait for confirmation of a theft before acting if there is credible evidence that your recovery phrase has been compromised.

evidence.title: Ledger CryptoBilis Hack Explained: $93M Stolen, Wallets Tampered
evidence.evidence_text:
French hardware-wallet manufacturer Ledger is investigating a suspected supply-chain attack involving Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis after blockchain researchers traced an estimated $93.2 million in cryptocurrency stolen from 315 wallets across six networks on October 9.
The investigation has uncovered an unauthorized hardware implant inside at least one affected Ledger device, while security researchers have separately reported suspicious modifications in wallets purchased through other retailers. CryptoBilis has suspended hardware-wallet sales in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines as questions mount over the origin of the compromised devices.
On October 10, Ledger confirmed finding an unauthorized hardware implant in an affected customer’s device. Its October 11 update said the confirmed cases associated with the October 9 draining incident involved purchases through CryptoBilis, and that Ledger’s own systems and direct sales channels remained unaffected.
The investigation has also drawn attention to CryptoBilis’ ownership after its former founders disclosed that they handed over operational control to new management in March 2026, months before the thefts.
How the $93 Million Ledger Wallet Theft Unfolded
The first coordinated wallet-draining transactions began on October 9, with attackers targeting wallets holding Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT and other cryptocurrencies.
According to Bitquery’s on-chain investigation, the suspected attacker had been preparing the operation since late September. Addresses associated with the theft received initial funding on September 25, followed by 21 small test transactions on TRON and another 20 on Ethereum between September 26 and October 7.
At approximately 04:59 UTC on October 9, the attacker changed the account permissions of 30 TRON wallets, granting a common key control over their funds. Coordinated withdrawals started shortly afterward across Ethereum, BNB Chain, Polygon, Solana, and Bitcoin.
On Bitcoin, approximately 203.8 BTC was transferred from 111 addresses in a single block at around 05:54 UTC, according to the investigation.
Bitquery’s October 11 assessment identified $93.2 million in suspected thefts from 315 wallets across six networks. TRON accounted for approximately $70.5 million, followed by $16.8 million in Bitcoin and $3.7 million in Ethereum. The remaining funds were traced across BNB Chain, Polygon, and Solana.
The estimates have increased as investigators identified additional affected addresses. As The Crypto Times initially reported on October 9, on-chain researcher Specter had estimated losses exceeding $86 million across several networks when Ledger first acknowledged the complaints.
Ledger has not confirmed Bitquery’s latest total or publicly disclosed the final number of affected customers.
Ledger Confirms Hidden Hardware Implant
Ledger acknowledged the incident on October 9 after receiving reports of missing funds from customers who had purchased devices through CryptoBilis. In its initial statement, the company asked the reseller to suspend sales and shipments while its investigation continued.
Customers who had purchased devices from CryptoBilis within the preceding 90 days were advised not to initialize unused products. Those who had already configured their wallets were urged to consider transferring their assets to a new trusted device using a newly generated recovery phrase.
On October 10, Ledger confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant inside one affected device.
The discovery strengthened concerns about physical tampering, which had emerged after former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès shared details of a suspicious component found in a separate Ledger wallet. The Crypto Times reported Ledger’s confirmation on October 11, noting that the discovery did not establish how every affected wallet had been compromised.
Hardware wallets are designed to isolate private keys from internet-connected devices. During initialization, however, recovery words appear on the device’s screen. Researchers investigating the modified hardware have described implants positioned to intercept the screen’s internal communications.
Such a component could potentially capture a recovery phrase during setup, allowing an attacker to recreate the wallet elsewhere and withdraw its assets without obtaining the original device.
Ledger has not confirmed that every stolen wallet was compromised through this mechanism.
Mark Karpelès and Researchers Report Additional Tampered Wallets
Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès reported on October 9 that he had examined a Ledger device shipped from Malaysia with an apparently intact external seal but a concealed component near its display.
Karpelès subsequently shared microscope images and described the suspicious hardware as a miniature spy SIM card. The component was reportedly installed beneath the screen assembly, where it would be difficult for ordinary buyers to detect.
His examination raised concerns that modified hardware could reach customers in packaging that appeared undisturbed.
The Crypto Times covered Karpelès’ discovery and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao’s initial warning on October 10, before Ledger’s subsequent confirmation strengthened evidence of physical tampering in the CryptoBilis investigation.
Separate technical research published by Tibane Labs documented suspicious modifications in Ledger Nano X devices obtained through sellers in Japan, including hardware reportedly shipped from Malaysia.
Security researcher Johannes, posting under @0xJohannes_, reported finding what appeared to be an implant inside a Ledger purchased approximately two weeks earlier from electronics retailer MediaMarkt.
He said the modified device resembled an earlier version of the hardware described in the Southeast Asian reports. However, no funds had been stolen from his wallet.
Ledger has not established that the European device is connected to the October 9 incident. As The Crypto Times reported on October 12, the European findings remain separate from the confirmed CryptoBilis-linked cases. Similar physical modifications alone cannot establish that the devices share an attacker or distribution source.
CryptoBilis Suspends Sales as Former Founders Distance Themselves
Following Ledger’s warning, CryptoBilis suspended Ledger device sales and shipments before extending the halt to its hardware-wallet inventory.
Reports also described temporary closures of retail and online sales channels in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines while the company reviewed the incident and handled customer complaints.
The suspension followed growing concerns that devices could have been modified before reaching buyers.
Meanwhile, CryptoBilis’ former co-founders, Arravind Prabu and Vimalatheethan, released a statement explaining that they were no longer responsible for the company’s operations. According to their statement, CryptoBilis changed ownership earlier in 2026, with operational and administrative control transferred to new management in March.
The founders said they had not retained access to the company’s backend infrastructure, customer databases, order management systems or administrative accounts since the handover. They acknowledged some limited advisory involvement during industry events after the acquisition but denied having any role in its daily operations. The statement also disclosed that the acquisition agreement included confidentiality provisions delaying a joint public announcement until mid-October 2026.
The former founders identified Nicholas Chang as a contact for inquiries concerning current operations. The Crypto Times has also contacted Cryptobills and is awaiting a response from them.
Separately, reported corporate filings indicate that the reseller’s shares were transferred to new ownership in August 2026. The ownership transfer preceded the October theft, but no publicly verified evidence establishes a criminal connection between the acquisition and the tampered devices.
CZ Questions CryptoBilis Acquisition as Investigation Expands
Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, commonly known as CZ, was among the first prominent industry figures to react publicly to the reports. On October 9, he suggested that the early evidence pointed toward a supply-chain attack involving a particular vendor rather than a compromise across Ledger’s broader hardware-wallet ecosystem. He also encouraged efforts to trace and recover the stolen funds.
Zhao later made a stronger allegation after details of the CryptoBilis ownership transfer emerged.
In an October 12 post on X, CZ claimed that the hackers had apparently purchased the reseller and required a non-disclosure agreement.
The accusation linked two developments that had already attracted scrutiny: the reseller’s acquisition earlier in 2026 and the thefts in October.
However, while former management has acknowledged the ownership transfer and confidentiality agreement, no publicly disclosed evidence establishes that the buyer was associated with the attackers or that the acquisition was intended to facilitate the theft.

evidence.title: Denial of service with failed call
evidence.evidence_text:
External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately, which can cause a denial of service in the contract. When a contract needs every call in a batch to succeed, for example payments pushed to many recipients in a loop, one failing recipient can block the whole operation. The Solidity documentation adds that sending Ether can fail because the recipient runs out of gas, including through require, assert or revert, and that with transfer or send plus a return value check this can give the recipient a way to block progress in the sending contract.
Root cause: Progress depends on every external transfer or call succeeding. Isolate each external call into its own transaction that can be initiated by the recipient of the call. This matters especially for payments: let users withdraw funds rather than pushing funds to them automatically, which also reduces the chance of problems with the gas limit. Avoid combining multiple calls in a single transaction, especially inside a loop, always assume external calls can fail, and implement the contract logic to handle failed calls.

evidence.title: Flash loan facilitated attacks
evidence.evidence_text:
A flash loan is uncollateralized, same-transaction borrowing. OWASP says flash loans are not inherently vulnerable, but they give an attacker arbitrarily large, transient capital within one transaction. Any protocol whose trust assumptions rest on capital at risk or historical position size is exposed when an attacker can hold large balances temporarily without risking their own funds. The attacker batches a transaction that borrows via a flash loan, manipulates protocol state, prices or accounting with the borrowed funds, extracts profit, and repays the loan in the same transaction. OWASP names governance voting, oracle pricing, share and accounting logic, and liquidation and collateral checks as areas to review.
Root cause: Protocol assumptions fail when an attacker temporarily controls substantial liquidity. OWASP notes that flash loans act as a force multiplier for underlying business logic, oracle, arithmetic or access control weaknesses, which must be fixed at the root. Design economic and accounting logic on the assumption that arbitrarily large, transient capital is available. Rate limit sensitive operations per block or epoch, cap exposure per interaction with limits on slippage, position sizes and borrowing, and include flash-loan scenarios in tests and fuzzing.

evidence.title: Unprotected Ether withdrawal
evidence.evidence_text:
Due to missing or insufficient access controls, malicious parties can withdraw some or all Ether from the contract account. The SWC entry notes that this bug is sometimes caused by unintentionally exposing initialization functions: if a function intended to be a constructor is named wrongly, its code ends up in the runtime bytecode and can be called by anyone to re-initialize the contract. Before Solidity 0.4.22 a constructor was a function named exactly like its contract, so a name mismatch left it a normal callable function.
Root cause: Withdrawal functions lack effective caller authorization, so the contract does not check who may trigger a transfer of Ether out. Implement controls so withdrawals can only be triggered by authorized parties or according to the specs of the smart contract system. Also check that initialization code cannot be called again by an arbitrary account. Since Solidity 0.4.22 the constructor keyword makes constructor definitions clearer than the old same-name rule. The SWC registry is no longer actively maintained, so treat its text as historical guidance.

evidence.title: Incorrect constructor name
evidence.evidence_text:
Constructors are special functions called only once, during contract creation. They perform critical, privileged actions such as setting the owner of the contract. Before Solidity 0.4.22, the only way to define a constructor was a function with the same name as the contract. A function meant to be a constructor becomes a normal callable function if its name does not exactly match the contract name, which can happen when contract code is re-used under a different name and the constructor function name is not changed. Since Solidity 0.4.22 the constructor keyword is available, and the Solidity documentation describes the constructor as a function declared with it that runs once at creation.
Root cause: A function intended as a constructor does not match the legacy contract name, so it stays callable after deployment. Upgrade the contract to a recent Solidity compiler version and change to the constructor keyword declaration, which makes constructor definitions clearer.

evidence.title: Reentrancy
evidence.evidence_text:
External calls can reenter before state is finalized. Calling another contract hands it control, allowing it to call back before the first call returns. In a withdrawal that sends Ether before clearing the caller balance, a callback can withdraw against the still-unchanged balance again. Reentrancy can arise from calls to other contracts, not only Ether transfers; dependencies across multiple contracts also matter.
Root cause: State updates after untrusted calls allow repeated execution. Apply checks-effects-interactions: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage state, then make external calls. In the withdrawal example, save the withdrawal amount and clear the stored balance before calling the recipient; require the call to succeed so failure reverts the operation. Review other callable paths and contracts sharing the affected state, since a callback may enter through another function or dependency.
